note.explanation: The modern periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Their electron arrangements explain their positions and help us understand repeating patterns in their properties.
examples: Sodium is in Period 3 and Group 1; it has one electron in its outermost shell.
Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period, while ionization energy generally increases.
note.simple: Elements are arranged by atomic number. Their properties repeat in a pattern because their outer-electron arrangements repeat.
note.checkQuestion: What determines the order of elements in the modern periodic table?
note.title: How the Periodic Table Organises Elements
steps: Use its electron arrangement to identify its period and group.
Use its position to predict trends such as atomic radius and metallic character.
note.answer: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number.

mcqs.stem: In which period and group will you place the element which is an important part of the solar cell?
rationales: Silicon is used in solar cells and is in the third period and 14th group.
This is not silicon's position; silicon is in the third period.
This is not silicon's group; silicon is in Group 14.
This is not silicon's group; silicon is in Group 14.

mcqs.stem: Identify the electronic configuration of the outermost shell of a transition metal.
rationales: This is a p-block valence-shell pattern, not the transition-metal pattern given here.
Transition metals have a partially filled d-subshell and two s electrons in the pattern ndˣns².
This is the configuration of a filled outer shell.
This is a p-block pattern with five p electrons.
Sodium is an alkali metal and is the softest choice listed.
Calcium is harder than sodium.
Aluminium is not as soft as sodium.
Zinc is not as soft as sodium.

mcqs.stem: A yellow solid element exists in allotropic forms which is also present in fossil fuels. Indicate the name.
rationales: Carbon has allotropes, but it is not the yellow solid described here.
Iodine is a solid, but it is not the yellow element described.
Aluminium is a metal, not the yellow allotrope-forming element described.
Sulphur is a yellow solid with allotropes and is present in fossil fuels.

mcqs.stem: How many electrons can nitrogen accept in its outermost shell?
rationales: Nitrogen needs three electrons to complete its outer shell, not two.
Nitrogen has five outer electrons and can accept three to complete an octet.
Accepting four would give nitrogen more than an octet in this simple model.
Five electrons is not the number needed to complete nitrogen's outer shell.

mcqs.stem: Which element is the most reactive element?
rationales: Oxygen is reactive, but fluorine is the most reactive element listed.
Chlorine is reactive, but is less reactive than fluorine.
Fluorine is the most reactive element listed.
Nitrogen is comparatively unreactive because of its strong triple bond.

mcqs.stem: Which element has the highest melting point?
rationales: Among these alkali metals, sodium has the highest melting point.
Potassium has a lower melting point than sodium.
Rubidium has a lower melting point than sodium.
Caesium has a lower melting point than sodium.

mcqs.stem: In what order does the metallic character change in the second group?
rationales: This does not show the steady increase down Group 2.
This order does not place the elements in increasing metallic character down the group.
This order incorrectly places strontium before calcium and barium.
Metallic character increases down Group 2, giving Ba > Sr > Ca > Mg.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following best describe the correct order of oxygen, fluorine, and nitrogen's atomic radii?
rationales: Fluorine is smaller than oxygen, so this order is incorrect.
Nitrogen has the largest radius of these three, so this order is incorrect.
Atomic radius decreases across the period from nitrogen to oxygen to fluorine.
Fluorine, not nitrogen, has the smallest radius of these three.

mcqs.stem: The element having less value of ionization energy and less value of electron affinity is likely to belong to:
rationales: Group 1 elements readily lose their single outer electron and generally have low ionization energy and electron affinity.
Group 13 is not the best match for both low values.
Group 16 elements generally have greater electron affinity than Group 1 elements.
Group 17 elements have high electron affinity, so this is not the best match.

written.text: Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?
written.finalAnswer: Atomic number, unlike atomic mass, gives the correct order of elements and their properties.

rubric.why: Identifies the basis for the modern arrangement.
rubric.description: State that the table is arranged by atomic number.
rubric.how: Write that elements are arranged in increasing atomic number.

rubric.why: Explains why atomic number is the suitable basis.
rubric.description: Connect atomic number with correct placement or periodic properties.
rubric.how: Explain that it gives the correct order and recurring properties.

modelAnswer: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Atomic number gives the correct order of elements and their properties, unlike atomic mass.

written.text: What is the significance of the word periodic?
written.finalAnswer: The properties of elements repeat periodically when the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.

rubric.why: States what repeats in the table.
rubric.description: Identify that element properties repeat.
rubric.how: Mention the repetition of properties.

rubric.why: Links the repetition to the periodic arrangement.
rubric.description: Connect repeating properties with arrangement by atomic number.
rubric.how: State that the repetition occurs when elements are arranged by increasing atomic number.

modelAnswer: When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, their properties repeat.
This repetition is the significance of the word periodic.

written.text: Why does the size of a period increase as we move down the periodic table?
written.finalAnswer: The number of elements in a period depends on the number of electrons that can occupy the available shells and subshells; these increase in the lower periods.

rubric.why: Recognises that period size is linked to electron capacity.
rubric.description: Relate the number of elements to electron-shell capacity.
rubric.how: Mention the shells or subshells that electrons occupy.

rubric.why: Explains why lower periods can contain more elements.
rubric.description: State that lower periods have more available electron capacity.
rubric.how: Explain that available shells or subshells can accommodate more electrons lower in the table.

modelAnswer: The number of elements in a period is related to the number of electrons that can occupy its shells and subshells.
These available electron positions increase in the lower periods, so period size increases.

written.text: In a group, the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell. Why is it so?
written.finalAnswer: Elements in the same group have similar outermost-shell electron arrangements, so they have the same number of outermost-shell electrons.

rubric.why: Gives the shared electron feature of a group.
rubric.description: State that group members share the number of outer electrons.
rubric.how: Mention the same number of electrons in the outermost shell.

rubric.why: Connects the shared arrangement to group membership.
rubric.description: Explain that similar outer-shell arrangements place elements together in a group.
rubric.how: Relate the outermost-shell electron arrangement to their position in the same group.

modelAnswer: Elements in the same group have similar electronic configurations in their outermost shells.
Therefore, they have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell.

written.text: Do you expect calcium to be more reactive than sodium? Give the reason of your answer.
written.finalAnswer: No. Sodium is more reactive than calcium because sodium loses its single outermost electron more readily.

rubric.why: Gives the correct comparison.
rubric.description: State whether calcium is more reactive than sodium.
rubric.how: Answer that sodium is more reactive.

rubric.why: Explains the comparison using electron loss.
rubric.description: Give a reason based on ease of losing outer electrons.
rubric.how: State that sodium loses its one outermost electron more readily.

modelAnswer: No, calcium is not more reactive than sodium.
Sodium loses its single outermost electron more readily than calcium loses its two outermost electrons.

written.text: Which element has the maximum atomic radius and which element has the minimum atomic radius in third period?
written.finalAnswer: Sodium has the maximum atomic radius and chlorine has the minimum atomic radius.

rubric.why: Identifies the largest atom in Period 3.
rubric.description: Name the element with maximum atomic radius.
rubric.how: Give sodium.

rubric.why: Identifies the smallest atom in Period 3.
rubric.description: Name the element with minimum atomic radius.
rubric.how: Give chlorine.

modelAnswer: Sodium has the maximum atomic radius in the third period.
Chlorine has the minimum atomic radius in the third period.

written.text: Why are the most electronegative elements present in sixth and seventh groups?
written.finalAnswer: Elements in Groups 16 and 17 need only two or one electrons respectively to complete their outer shells, so they strongly attract electrons.

rubric.why: Identifies the groups and their near-complete outer shells.
rubric.description: Relate these groups to their outer-shell electron numbers.
rubric.how: State that these elements need few electrons to complete the outer shell.

rubric.why: Explains the strong attraction for bonding electrons.
rubric.description: Link their need for electrons with electronegativity.
rubric.how: Explain that this makes them strongly attract electrons.

modelAnswer: The elements of the sixth and seventh groups have six and seven outermost-shell electrons respectively.
They need only two or one electrons to complete their shells and strongly attract electrons.

written.text: The first ionization energy value of magnesium is less than the second one. Give reason.
written.finalAnswer: After the first electron is removed, Mg⁺ has a positive charge and holds its remaining electrons more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove the second electron.

rubric.why: Recognises the ion formed after the first ionisation.
rubric.description: State that magnesium becomes a positive ion after losing one electron.
rubric.how: Write that Mg becomes Mg⁺.

rubric.why: Explains why the second removal requires more energy.
rubric.description: Explain the increased attraction on the remaining electrons.
rubric.how: State that the positive ion holds its remaining electrons more strongly.

modelAnswer: After losing its first electron, magnesium forms Mg⁺.
The remaining electrons are attracted more strongly, so more energy is required to remove the second electron.

written.text: Is it possible for two metals or two non-metals to form an ionic bond?
written.finalAnswer: Usually, no. An ionic bond is generally formed by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.

rubric.why: Gives the general conclusion for the stated pairs.
rubric.description: Answer whether two metals or two non-metals generally form an ionic bond.
rubric.how: State that they usually do not.

rubric.why: States the electron-transfer basis of ionic bonding.
rubric.description: Explain the usual metal-to-non-metal electron transfer.
rubric.how: Mention electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal.

modelAnswer: Usually, two metals or two non-metals do not form an ionic bond with each other.
An ionic bond is generally formed by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.

written.text: Which element has the least value of ionization energy and which element has the highest value of electronegativity?
written.finalAnswer: Francium has the least ionization energy and fluorine has the highest electronegativity.

rubric.why: Identifies the element with the least ionization energy.
rubric.description: Name the element with the least ionization energy.
rubric.how: Give francium.

rubric.why: Identifies the most electronegative element.
rubric.description: Name the element with the highest electronegativity.
rubric.how: Give fluorine.

modelAnswer: Francium has the least value of ionization energy.
Fluorine has the highest value of electronegativity.

written.text: Suppose a new element is discovered. Where would you like to accommodate this element in the periodic table?
written.finalAnswer: Place it according to its atomic number and electronic configuration, in the period and group matching its shells and outermost electrons.

rubric.why: Uses the modern periodic table's ordering rule.
rubric.description: Locate the new element using its atomic number.
rubric.how: State that it should be placed in order of increasing atomic number.

rubric.why: Uses electron arrangement to identify its table position.
rubric.description: Use shells and outer electrons to determine period and group.
rubric.how: Explain that its electronic configuration indicates the suitable period and group.

modelAnswer: Find the atomic number and electronic configuration of the new element.
Place it in order of increasing atomic number.
Use the number of occupied shells to find its period.
Use its outermost-shell electrons to find its group.

written.text: What is the first element of the periodic table? Will it lose an electron or gain it?
written.finalAnswer: Hydrogen is the first element. It may lose one electron or gain one electron.

rubric.why: Identifies the first element correctly.
rubric.description: Name the first element of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Write hydrogen.

rubric.why: Recognises hydrogen's possible electron behaviour.
rubric.description: State whether hydrogen loses or gains an electron.
rubric.how: Explain that it may lose one electron or gain one electron.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen is the first element of the periodic table.
It has one electron and may lose one electron.
It may also gain one electron to attain a stable arrangement.

written.text: Atomic radii of boron and aluminum are 88 pm and 125 pm respectively. Which element is expected to lose electron or electrons easily?
written.finalAnswer: Aluminium; its larger atomic radius means its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.

rubric.why: Selects the element with the larger given radius.
rubric.description: Compare the two radii and identify the element expected to lose electrons more easily.
rubric.how: Choose aluminium, whose radius is 125 pm.

rubric.why: Explains the relationship between atomic size and electron loss.
rubric.description: Use the greater distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus as the reason.
rubric.how: Explain that aluminium's outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and easier to remove.

modelAnswer: Radius of boron = 88 pm; radius of aluminium = 125 pm.
Aluminium has the larger atomic radius.
Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.
Therefore, aluminium is expected to lose electron or electrons easily.

written.text: How would you find the atomic radius of an atom?
written.finalAnswer: Measure the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms and take half of that distance.

rubric.why: Identifies the distance used to determine atomic radius.
rubric.description: Describe measuring between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.
rubric.how: State that the nucleus-to-nucleus distance is measured.

rubric.why: Gives the required relationship between that distance and radius.
rubric.description: Explain that the atomic radius is half the internuclear distance.
rubric.how: Take half the measured distance.

modelAnswer: Measure the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.
The atomic radius is half of this distance.

written.text: Why is it not possible for oxygen atom to accept three electrons to form O³⁻ ion like nitrogen which can accept electrons to form N³⁻?
written.finalAnswer: Oxygen has six outermost-shell electrons and needs two, not three, to complete its octet; accepting three would exceed the octet.

rubric.why: Identifies oxygen's valence electrons and the number needed for completion.
rubric.description: State that oxygen has six outer electrons and needs two more.
rubric.how: Mention its six outermost-shell electrons and the two-electron requirement.

rubric.why: Explains why gaining three is not suitable.
rubric.description: Explain that three additional electrons would exceed a stable octet.
rubric.how: State that oxygen completes its octet by gaining two, not three.

modelAnswer: Oxygen has six electrons in its outermost shell and needs two electrons to complete its octet.
If it accepted three electrons, it would have more than an octet in its outermost shell.
Therefore, oxygen does not form O³⁻ like nitrogen forms N³⁻.

written.text: Which information is needed to locate the elements in the periodic table if you do not know its atomic number? Is atomic mass helpful for this purpose?
written.finalAnswer: The electronic configuration is needed to find the period and group. Atomic mass is not a reliable way to locate an element; atomic number gives its correct position.

rubric.why: Identifies the electron information that indicates an element's position.
rubric.description: Use electronic configuration to identify period and group.
rubric.how: State that the configuration gives the number of shells and outer electrons.

rubric.why: Distinguishes atomic mass from the reliable modern ordering rule.
rubric.description: Explain whether atomic mass is useful and identify atomic number as the correct basis.
rubric.how: State that mass is not reliable for placement and atomic number determines the correct order.

modelAnswer: The electronic configuration is needed to locate an element if its atomic number is not known.
The number of occupied shells gives its period, and its outermost-shell electrons help identify its group.
Atomic mass is not a reliable basis for the arrangement.
Atomic number gives the correct order of elements.

written.text: How many blocks of elements are present in the periodic table? Are these blocks helpful in studying the properties of elements?
written.finalAnswer: There are four blocks: s, p, d and f. Yes; they help study elements according to the subshell being filled and their related properties.

rubric.why: Names the number and labels of the blocks.
rubric.description: Give the four blocks of the periodic table.
rubric.how: List s, p, d and f.

rubric.why: Explains the value of block classification.
rubric.description: Connect the blocks with electron configuration and properties.
rubric.how: State that blocks group elements by the subshell being filled, helping study their properties.

modelAnswer: There are four blocks of elements in the periodic table: s, p, d and f.
Yes, these blocks help in studying properties because they show which subshell is being filled.

written.text: Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (a) Atomic radius
written.finalAnswer: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period because nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same shell, so they are attracted more strongly.

rubric.why: States the trend across a period correctly.
rubric.description: Describe how atomic radius changes across a period.
rubric.how: State that it generally decreases from left to right.

rubric.why: Explains the trend using nuclear attraction.
rubric.description: Explain the effect of increased nuclear charge on electrons in the same shell.
rubric.how: State that added protons attract same-shell electrons more strongly.

modelAnswer: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases from left to right.
The nuclear charge increases, but added electrons enter the same shell.
The stronger attraction between the nucleus and electrons pulls the electrons closer.

written.text: Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (b) Ionization energy
written.finalAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period because atomic radius decreases and the nucleus attracts the outer electrons more strongly.

rubric.why: States the general trend correctly.
rubric.description: Describe how ionization energy changes across a period.
rubric.how: State that it generally increases from left to right.

rubric.why: Explains the trend through the stronger attraction to outer electrons.
rubric.description: Relate increased nuclear attraction and smaller atomic size to electron removal.
rubric.how: State that outer electrons are held more strongly and need more energy to remove.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
Atomic radius decreases and the nuclear attraction on the outer electrons becomes stronger.
Therefore, more energy is needed to remove an outer electron.

written.text: Which physical properties of elements may lead us to know what type of bond it will form?
written.finalAnswer: Electronegativity and ionization energy help predict the bond type, since they indicate an atom's tendency to attract or lose electrons.

rubric.why: Names relevant properties used to predict bonding.
rubric.description: Identify physical properties that indicate electron behaviour.
rubric.how: Give electronegativity and ionization energy.

rubric.why: Explains how those properties inform bond prediction.
rubric.description: Connect the properties to electron transfer or sharing.
rubric.how: Explain that they show an atom's tendency to attract or lose electrons.

modelAnswer: Electronegativity and ionization energy may help us predict the type of bond an element forms.
They indicate how strongly an atom attracts electrons and how readily it loses them.

written.text: Write down the names of four non-metals which exist in solid state at normal temperature.
written.finalAnswer: Carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.

rubric.why: Gives examples of solid non-metals.
rubric.description: Name solid non-metals at normal temperature.
rubric.how: List any valid solid non-metals.

rubric.why: Completes the required set of four examples.
rubric.description: Give four correct names in total.
rubric.how: Include four of carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.

modelAnswer: Carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine are four non-metals that exist as solids at normal temperature.

written.text: Why do second and third periods have equal number of elements while all other periods contain different number of elements?
written.finalAnswer: The second and third periods each have two s-block and six p-block elements, making eight; other periods also include d- or f-block elements and have different capacities.

rubric.why: States the equal size and basic block count of Periods 2 and 3.
rubric.description: Explain that each of these periods contains eight elements.
rubric.how: State that each has two s-block and six p-block elements.

rubric.why: Explains why other periods have different lengths.
rubric.description: Relate the other period lengths to additional subshells and capacities.
rubric.how: Mention that d- and f-block elements occur in other periods, changing their numbers of elements.

modelAnswer: The second and third periods each contain eight elements.
Each has two s-block elements and six p-block elements.
Other periods have different numbers of elements because d- and f-subshells are also filled in them.
These subshells have different capacities, so the periods have different lengths.

written.text: Arrangement of the elements in the form of a periodic table is a remarkable achievement of chemists. Comment on this statement citing the benefits of this table.
written.finalAnswer: The periodic table organises elements systematically, shows repeating patterns in their properties, and allows properties of elements to be compared and predicted from their positions.

rubric.why: Explains the table's organising benefit.
rubric.description: Describe how the table systematically arranges elements.
rubric.how: State that it arranges elements in an orderly way according to atomic number.

rubric.why: Explains how the arrangement helps with understanding and prediction.
rubric.description: Mention recurring trends and prediction or comparison of properties.
rubric.how: Explain that positions show periodic trends and help compare or predict properties.

modelAnswer: The periodic table arranges all known elements systematically according to increasing atomic number.
Elements with similar outer electronic configurations are placed in the same groups.
Their positions show periodic repetition and trends in properties.
This arrangement makes it easier to compare elements and predict the properties of an element from its position.

written.text: Both lithium and beryllium show behaviour different from rest of the alkali and alkaline earth metals respectively. Can you think of the possible reasons for this difference?
written.finalAnswer: Lithium and beryllium are unusually small and have high charge density and relatively high ionization energies; their small size gives them behaviour different from the other members of their groups.

rubric.why: Identifies the unusual small size of the first members.
rubric.description: Give the small atomic or ionic size as a cause.
rubric.how: State that lithium and beryllium are much smaller than the other group members.

rubric.why: Connects size with their distinctive chemical behaviour.
rubric.description: Explain the resulting strong attraction, high charge density or ionization energy.
rubric.how: Describe how their small size produces distinctive properties compared with the rest of each group.

modelAnswer: Lithium and beryllium have very small atomic and ionic sizes compared with the other members of their groups.
Their small size gives them high charge density and strong attraction for electrons.
Their ionization energies and chemical behaviour therefore differ from those of the other alkali and alkaline earth metals.

written.text: Modern periodic table is the amended form of the earlier table developed by Mandeleev. Elaborate how these two tables are different from each other.
written.finalAnswer: Mendeleev arranged elements mainly by atomic mass and chemical properties, while the modern table arranges them by increasing atomic number and explains periodicity through electronic configuration.

rubric.why: Describes the basis of Mendeleev's table.
rubric.description: State how Mendeleev arranged the elements.
rubric.how: Mention atomic mass and similarities in chemical properties.

rubric.why: Contrasts the modern basis and explains the modern table's strength.
rubric.description: State the modern arrangement and its connection to periodicity.
rubric.how: Mention increasing atomic number and the role of electronic configuration.

modelAnswer: Mendeleev arranged elements mainly in order of increasing atomic mass and placed elements with similar chemical properties together.
The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number.
The modern arrangement removes inconsistencies that arose when atomic mass was used.
The periodic repetition of properties is explained by the repetition of electronic configurations.

examTips: Section A may test element positions, electron configurations and periodic trends; learn the exact trend and the reason behind it.
Short questions usually need a direct fact plus one clear reason, such as why radius changes across a period.
Constructed-response and descriptive questions often ask you to compare two elements or explain a trend using electron arrangement and nuclear attraction.
For written explanations, state the trend first, then give the cause; this helps earn both result and reasoning marks.
Use correct terms such as atomic number, outermost shell, ionization energy and electronegativity.

hints: Recall the direction of atomic-radius change across a period.
Across a period, nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell; identify the two endpoint elements of Period 3.
yourTurn.question: Which element has the maximum atomic radius and which element has the minimum atomic radius in third period?
solution: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases from left to right.
The third period begins with sodium and ends with chlorine among the elements asked about.
Therefore, sodium has the maximum atomic radius and chlorine has the minimum atomic radius.
yourTurn.answer: Sodium has the maximum atomic radius and chlorine has the minimum atomic radius.

hints: Compare the two radii given in the question.
The element with the larger radius holds its outer electrons less strongly, so consider which value is 125 pm.
yourTurn.question: Atomic radii of boron and aluminum are 88 pm and 125 pm respectively. Which element is expected to lose electron or electrons easily?
solution: Radius of boron = 88 pm; radius of aluminium = 125 pm.
Aluminium has the larger atomic radius.
Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.
Therefore, aluminium is expected to lose electron or electrons easily.
yourTurn.answer: Aluminium; its larger atomic radius means its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.

steps.text: Radius of boron = 88 pm; radius of aluminium = 125 pm.

steps.why: A larger atomic radius means the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.
steps.text: Aluminium has the larger atomic radius.

steps.why: Electrons farther from the nucleus are held less strongly and are easier to remove.
steps.text: Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.

steps.why: This follows directly from the comparison and answers which element loses electrons more easily.
steps.text: Therefore, aluminium is expected to lose electron or electrons easily.

example.question: Atomic radii of boron and aluminum are 88 pm and 125 pm respectively. Which element is expected to lose electron or electrons easily?
example.answer: Aluminium; its larger atomic radius means its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.

explain.title: The modern periodic table
explain.body: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. The electronic configuration helps determine an element's period, group and block.

explain.title: Periods, groups and blocks
explain.body: A period is a horizontal row and a group is a vertical column. Elements in a group have related outer-shell arrangements. The four blocks are s, p, d and f.

explain.title: Periodic trends
explain.body: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases and ionization energy generally increases. Down a group, atomic size and metallic character generally increase.

explain.title: Electrons and bonding
explain.body: Metals tend to lose electrons, while non-metals tend to gain or attract electrons. Ionic bonding generally involves electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal.

explain.title: Using the table
explain.body: The periodic table helps organise elements, compare their properties and predict behaviour from their positions and electron arrangements.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic number with atomic mass; the modern table is arranged by atomic number.
Do not reverse the across-period trends: atomic radius generally decreases, while ionization energy generally increases.
When explaining a trend, include its reason, not only the direction of change.
Do not say oxygen accepts three electrons; it needs two electrons to complete its outer shell.
Write both the comparison and the reason when a question asks for a reason.
